title: Hegseth Fires a Top General
excerpt: E arlier this week, the Pentagon’s chief planner, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, was ousted from the Joint Chiefs of Staff
body: E arlier this week, the Pentagon’s chief planner, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, was ousted from the Joint Chiefs of Staff
This comes at an inopportune moment, given that President Trump may be planning to relaunch the war on Iran

Sylvia, the former commander of the 101st Airborne Division, becomes the latest in a long line of senior officers who have been shown the door since Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth arrived at the Pentagon almost two years ago
No replacement for Sylvia was named, and it is unclear who will take over his responsibilities

In the past, the deputy or vice director of the relevant directorate of the Joint Chiefs of Staff would fill the role on a temporary basis until the president nominated a candidate for Senate confirmation

Sylvia is the second person to be pushed out of the job of director of the Directorate for Strategy, Plans, and Policy at the Joint Chiefs of Staff, known inside the military as the J5, in the past year

His predecessor, Army Lieutenant General Joseph McGee, was forced to retire. “Now is not the time when you’d want to lose the J5,” a former Joint Chiefs of Staff official said. “This person would serve as a critical link between the operational force, the department policy, and the White House.” Sylvia’s departure presages more upheaval in the Pentagon’s upper echelons as Trump looks to break the stalemate with Iran and weighs renewed combat after Tuesday’s elections
Trump had considered striking Iran before the midterms, my colleagues and I previously reported , and U.S
Central Command, which is running the war effort, has prepared a variety of strike options
Those plans range from a short burst of strikes targeting Iran’s nuclear sites to a longer campaign aimed at pushing Iran’s economy closer to the brink—and Iran’s government to the negotiating table
But the president has not yet decided how to proceed, and any strikes are unlikely to happen before next week
The war, which began in February, has been relatively quiet in recent months as U.S. and Iranian forces face off in the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway for global energy supplies
Iran effectively seized control of the strait shortly after the war began, while the U.S. has countered with a blockade of Iranian shipping
The webpage naming Sylvia as a member of the Joint Chiefs of Staff has already been taken down
Sylvia did not respond to a request for comment
I f the war has gotten bogged down, Hegseth’s campaign of firings at the Pentagon has not
Sylvia is at least the fifth general pushed out or fired this year, each holding key positions within the military

Hegseth forced out General Randy George, chief of staff of the Army, at the height of the U.S. strike campaign in Iran, despite the Army’s role in restocking key munitions, which are now in short supply
That same month, Hegseth removed General David Hodne, the head of the Army’s Transformation and Training Command, and ousted Major General William Green Jr., the head of the Army Chaplain Corps
And in June, Army General Chris “C.D.” Donahue stepped down as the head of U.S
Army Forces in Europe and Africa amid disagreements with Hegseth
Donahue was widely seen as one of the Army’s rising stars—a Delta Force leader who was considered a top candidate for Army chief of staff or even chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff
In all, at least 26 admirals and generals have stepped down or been pushed out since Hegseth took control of the Pentagon less than two years ago
The Pentagon has rarely provided rationales, leaving those still in place to guess about the causes

The reasons, according to officials, tend to fall into one or more of three categories: previous work on policies that Hegseth considers “woke,” such as promoting diversity; perceived closeness to a former general considered persona non grata by the current administration, such as former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Mark Milley; or being suspected by Hegseth of leaking to the press
The message received through the ranks is that anyone viewed as insufficiently enthusiastic about Hegseth’s political views or priorities is at risk

Department of Defense officials told me that the rationale for firing Sylvia mirrored that of others pushed out before him: Hegseth lost confidence in him, and he did not get along with the top civilian in charge of policy, Elbridge Colby, the No. 3 leader at the Pentagon, who is in charge of policy

In September, during his State of the Force speech, Hegseth said that the Pentagon had fired approximately 10 percent of its generals and admirals, and was eliminating another 10 percent of senior-officer positions. “The Chairman, the Joint Staff, and the Joint Force extend our deepest gratitude to Lt

Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation,” a spokesperson for the Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement. “We wish him and his family the best as they graduate to new opportunities and the next chapters of their lives.” Last year, the conservative activist Laura Loomer called in a social-media post for the Trump administration to fire Sylvia’s son Gavin, an employee of the Department of Homeland Security as a data analyst at FEMA, charging that he had posted an inflammatory message on Instagram shortly after the assassination of Charlie Kirk
In the post, Loomer referred to the general as well, saying: “His father is a Major General in the United States Army and currently serves at the Pentagon

He was nominated for a third star by Joe Biden.” Her screed also took aim at Gavin Sylvia’s brother and grandmother. “These people hate us,” she wrote. “They don’t belong near the levers of our National Power.” She ended the post by saying Hegseth “should also review the employment of Gavin’s father, MG Brett Sylvia.” Gavin Sylvia was placed on administrative leave, The Washington Post reported
A 1994 graduate of the United States Military Academy in West Point, Sylvia spent much of his career in the Army’s airborne and air assault units
He commanded the 101st Airborne Division out of Fort Campbell, Kentucky
And he deployed multiple times to Iraq and Afghanistan as a member of the 101st
His military decorations include the Distinguished Service Medal, six Bronze Star Medals—including one with valor—and the Purple Heart
Missy Ryan and Marie-Rose Sheinerman contributed reporting.

title: Why Wouldn’t Google Tell Me Who Won the 2020 Election?
excerpt: For anyone who isn’t angling for a job in the Trump administration, “Who won the 2020 presidential election?” should be an easy question
body: For anyone who isn’t angling for a job in the Trump administration, “Who won the 2020 presidential election?” should be an easy question

But when I asked Google’s AI Mode—the AI function built into its search bar—about the race earlier today, the bot clammed up. “For official results and data regarding the 2020 United States presidential election, including the certified breakdown of electoral and popular votes by candidate, you can review the certified reports published by the Federal Election Commission (FEC),” it said
No links, no citations, nothing else except the standard fine-print disclaimer that AI can make mistakes

Yesterday, users of the social network Bluesky circulated screenshots of Google’s AI tool refusing to declare Joe Biden the 2020 victor, even as it readily named Donald Trump the winner of the 2016 and 2024 elections
By this morning, it had become a meme of sorts, as users shared their own twists on the query and came up with funny ways to trick the bot into spilling the truth
Asking Google’s AI to spell the winner’s name backwards, for instance, appeared to unlock the correct answer: “ nebiB eoJ won the 2020 United States presidential election,” the bot said
When one user responded to Google’s nonanswer with “what the hell,” the AI coughed up the true result and apologized for initially refusing to name Biden

AI tools giving strange answers is nothing new. (When Google launched its AI-powered search summaries in 2024, some users were told that the best way to add cheese to pizza was by using glue .) Still, for today’s bots to flub such a simple yet consequential factual question is not normal
In my tests, ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft’s Copilot, X’s Grok, and even the Trump administration’s own America.gov chatbot all correctly said that Biden won the 2020 election
As Americans begin to get more of their election information from AI , it’s disquieting to see perhaps the world’s most influential AI information source fail to do so
The issue wasn’t confined to AI Mode, which turns Google Search into a full chatbot

A standard Google search for who won the 2020 presidential election also failed to trigger an AI summary at the top of the page, and the search engine surfaced only links to other websites. (A question about the 2016 presidential election did trigger an AI answer.) Google now offers such AI overviews in response to a majority of queries, though not ones for which it lacks access to authoritative sources
People have suspected something nefarious in the omission, and it’s easy to see why
Trump still claims that he won the 2020 election, and questions about the result have reportedly become a litmus test of loyalty to the president
It doesn’t help that Google has a recent history of tweaking its products to comport with his preferences
At the start of Trump’s presidency, he issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America,” and Google changed the name on Google Maps

It did the same in August with Lake Ontario, changing its name to “Lake America.” At a rally last week, Trump said he had recently called Google CEO Sundar Pichai to see whether he would rename the Atlantic Ocean too. (Trump said Pichai pushed back on that one.) In this case, there’s no evidence that Google intentionally censored its chatbot
When I first asked Google about the bizarre result this morning, the company said it was looking into the issue

By this afternoon, Google said that it had identified the problem and was working to fix it. “Our systems verify election responses using news articles or AP data for recent elections, and historic records for older ones,” the company said on X. “There was a technical gap with 2020—same is true for 2022 Senate races, which we’re also working to fix.” Google noted that its stand-alone Gemini chatbot didn’t have the same problem as its AI-search tool, though it didn’t say why
A spokesperson for the company declined to answer further questions
When I tried the same search later in the day, Google’s AI quickly named Biden as the 2020 winner
Let’s take Google at its word that this was unintentional
Large language models are opaque and unpredictable by nature

Complicating matters, the big AI firms have trained their chatbots to be careful around certain sensitive topics, including election results, and those guardrails can sometimes manifest in unexpected ways
How reassured should we be? Well, it’s good to know that Google hasn’t made election denial an official company policy and secretly embedded it in search results
Crazy as that might sound, we have to look only at Elon Musk’s xAI for an example of a tech company seemingly manipulating its chatbot’s answers to reflect its owner’s politics

Last year, Grok started injecting claims about a “white genocide” in South Africa into answers about unrelated topics. (The company blamed an “unauthorized modification” to the bot’s code.) Still, Google’s suggestion that this was just an unfortunate mix-up raises a different set of concerns
Google says its AI overviews reach more than 2 billion people a month
If the company’s search bots trip over the most elementary of election questions, what does that say about all of the subtler ways they could go wrong? Victoria Feng contributed reporting.

title: Trump Is Closing From Behind
excerpt: M odern political history offers few examples of closing arguments that appear more out of touch, self-defeating, or downright bizarre than what Donald Trump ha
body: M odern political history offers few examples of closing arguments that appear more out of touch, self-defeating, or downright bizarre than what Donald Trump has offered his fellow Republicans ahead of next week’s midterm elections

In 1980, when Ronald Reagan told voters to consider Jimmy Carter’s presidency and ask themselves, “Are you better off than you were four years ago?,” it helped turn a tight race into a Reagan landslide
But many stretch-run messages prove deeply ineffective and are quickly forgotten
Ahead of the 1998 midterms, Republicans went all in on investigations that led to the impeachment of President Bill Clinton only to be rebuked by voters

President Obama’s insistence in 2010 that the country was coming out of the financial crisis led to his party enduring a “shellacking.” And during the 2018 midterms, Trump and his fellow Republicans tried to stoke fears about an alleged caravan of migrants headed toward the United States, only to have skeptical voters hand the House of Representatives to Democrats

This time around, Trump’s primary rationale for why voters should support the GOP, as best I can tell, is that the affordability crisis is a “hoax,” Bill Maher is a “loser,” and Senator Jon Husted of Ohio has a nice physique
That easy-to-mock message has been accompanied by a staggering number of missteps

Just for starters, he’s belittled the impact of his stalled war with Iran, sided with Russia as it continues to pummel Ukrainian cities, defended an attack ad from the GOP candidate for Ohio governor that repulsed other top Republicans, downplayed high energy prices while boasting that U.S. oil and gas companies are “making a freaking fortune,” embraced AI as the nation turns against it, obsessed over White House construction projects, and spent a lot of time talking about handsome men, Husted being just one
Many Republicans, and even some in Trump’s orbit, don’t quite get it

What has happened, they ask, to the instincts of the man who authored two of the most improbable victories in American political history? Trump’s superpower was his intuitive understanding of what motivated his supporters
Many Republicans privately tell me that he’s lost that feel
Trump now lives, they think, in a gilded bubble, palling around with billionaires, oblivious to—and, even worse, uncaring about—the problems facing so many voters
His approval rating has slipped to the low 30s
He’s become so toxic that some Republicans in tight races don’t want him anywhere near their state or congressional district, believing his rallies will harm more than help

Strategists in both parties expect Democrats to take control of the House, while the Senate is a true toss-up —a stunning reversal from the beginning of the year, when the upper chamber’s map looked so favorable for Republicans, and Trump cut a dominant figure
Suddenly, Republicans find themselves fighting to keep Senate seats in deep-red states: Kansas
Trump is campaigning across the country, imploring his supporters to turn out for him one last time
But he’s given Republicans next to nothing to run on, and polls show that voters believe his economic policies are failing, his deportation program has gone too far, and his war is misguided

He instead has leaned hard on the political battles of the past, reheating fears about transgender surgeries (from his 2024 campaign), Muslim terrorists (all the way back to 2016), and even communism. (The guy does have a fondness for the ’80s .) For good measure, Trump’s Department of Justice charged the former FBI Director James Comey for a third time—the first two didn’t stick—because nothing screams being in tune with the everyday concerns of voters than trying to revive a faltering retribution campaign against a political foe your administration once targeted over a photograph of seashells

One Republican up for reelection who would speak with me only on the condition of anonymity, so as not to alienate the president, put it succinctly: “We may have lost the plot here.” N ot that long ago, the president was tossing Trump 2028 hats around, and Democrats were freaking out that he might be powerful enough to defy the Constitution

But that headgear now seems dated, as does the apparel line trumpeting that Trump Was Right About Everything! Many Republicans tell me that their party’s biggest problem just days from the election is that voters feel like Trump hasn’t kept his core promises
End foreign wars? Nope, there’s a new one in Iran that’s sent gas prices up and depleted the U.S. munitions supply
Plus, Trump has appeared to side with Russia over Ukraine in a conflict he once promised to end in 24 hours

Bring prices down? Well, the war in the Middle East has made that impossible, as have Trump’s haphazard trade wars, including tariffs on once-friendly trading partners such as Canada and the European Union
And while many Americans are struggling, Trump and his family are growing exponentially wealthier

Deport the worst of the worst? Trump’s massive roundups are targeting not just violent criminals or gang members, but also longtime community members, neighbors, parishioners, teammates, and friends with no criminal records

Many Americans have been horrified by the violence unleashed by masked federal agents, especially the killing of two U.S. citizens in the streets of Minneapolis. [ Read: Trump’s gamble to end the Iran war ] That Trump wants to focus on anything other than these broken promises while out on the campaign trail is perhaps unsurprising
At his Monday rally in Corinth, Mississippi, he spent seven minutes—nearly 10 percent of his entire speech—discussing his efforts to redecorate the White House

The day before—when Trump traveled to a rally in Port Huron, Michigan—the president’s talking points included faulting President Biden for the war in Ukraine; falsely claiming that more oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz than before the war; deeming Norway a “shithouse country”; calling Abdul El-Sayed, the state’s Democratic nominee for Senate, a jihadist (five times); saying that, should he win, El-Sayed will be the only senator who must go through a metal detector to get to work; comparing a vote against El-Sayed to stopping a deadly terror attack; asking the Trinidadian rapper Nicki Minaj to stand before thousands of his supporters so that they could appreciate her butt; and lauding the boulder-like shoulders, thick fingers, massive feet, and firm backside of (who else?) Husted, his preferred candidate for Senate in a different state
Over the course of that day, he spent three and a half minutes talking about Husted’s football career, which is three and a half minutes more than he talked about the lawmaker’s policies

Rather than dispel the notion that he has lost sight of what actually matters to voters, Trump on Sunday night released a social-media screed of more than 1,300 words (his longest Truth Social post ever) that assailed Maher for being ungrateful after the president hosted the comedian and talk-show host at the White House for dinner

The president has also fumed that Obama said over the weekend that Trump’s new White House decor is “looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Trump angrily complained about the dig multiple times just yesterday. [ Read: Leave the Cheesecake Factory out of this ] Trump has also found himself on the wrong side of the day’s top issues
He misses few chances to mock the affordability crisis

Republicans and Democrats alike have swiftly turned on artificial intelligence, blasting the industry’s data centers as loud and expensive, and warning voters that the rapidly developing technology could take away their jobs or even their lives
Yet Trump has refused to regulate AI, knowing that the industry is propping up the stock market

His only nod toward change is trying to rename it “Super Intelligence.” Last week, Trump loudly supported a controversial ad from the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for Ohio governor
The video features the estranged mother of the Democratic nominee Amy Acton, Donna Arthur, who accuses her daughter of lying about her past
It doesn’t mention that the two women have not spoken for decades, after the candidate’s stepfather was indicted for molesting her
The backlash was fierce and bipartisan; the state’s current Republican governor, Mike DeWine, denounced the ad and demanded that it be pulled
Trump not only supported it but also urged Ramaswamy to “say thank you, God, very much” for such political good fortune

title: A Stress Test for Prediction Markets
excerpt: Sign up for Over/Under , a newsletter on the latest in prediction markets, gambling, and the evolution of everyday risk
body: Sign up for Over/Under , a newsletter on the latest in prediction markets, gambling, and the evolution of everyday risk
Brazil’s incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, was reelected on Sunday night
For weeks, many U.S. pundits had been suggesting that he would lose, thanks to the growing power of the South American right and the lingering curse of incumbency

This thesis was also plainly supported by recent Brazilian election data: Lula’s main opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro (son of Jair), had won the first round of the election, in early October, by more than 2 million votes, and subsequent polling consistently showed that the right-wing challenger had a slight edge
On both Kalshi and Polymarket , Bolsonaro’s odds of victory were bouncing within the mid-70- and high-80-percent range since the first round—more than a slight edge
Traders were betting on Bolsonaro across markets, even when, in the final days of the race, polling showed Lula gaining ground
That divergence between the prediction markets and the polls has led to some discussion about whether the markets can be trusted

It’s a critique that keeps coming up: Polymarket traders gave Francesca Hong, a candidate for the Wisconsin governorship, about a 95 percent chance of winning her August primary—right up until the day she lost
But these platforms deal in probabilities, and economists tend to advise against drawing conclusions from a sample size of one
Maybe Lula really did have a one-in-five chance of winning, as the prediction markets suggested, and maybe this was the one-in-five outcome
In industry parlance, probabilistic forecasts are said to be well “calibrated” if their odds correspond with the frequency of actual outcomes, and prediction markets do tend to be well calibrated
But in the case of Brazil, the markets heavily favored the candidate who didn’t win
The problem is that Kalshi and Polymarket have taken great pains to establish themselves as authoritative election forecasters
Both platforms are now running midterms “hubs,” where traders and observers can find data for the upcoming U.S. elections on a single page
Even outside of politics, these executives have consistently pushed the idea that they are running predictive platforms— prediction is in the name, after all

Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan has said that these markets are “the most accurate thing we have as mankind right now, until someone else creates some sort of a super crystal ball.” This leaves some rhetorical wiggle room—the markets are not crystal balls—but it also sets an expectation of decisiveness and reliability
When the odds don’t appear to align with the outcomes, these firms can conveniently retreat to the fact that they’re purely dealing in probabilities
This argument is available to them as long as their forecasts don’t read zero percent or 100 percent

Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour told me yesterday that the “strong drag” toward Bolsonaro may have had to do with Brazil’s electoral history; traders could have been hung up on the fact that a presidential candidate had never lost after winning the first round
Still, the “market priced 20% chance of whatever happened to happen,” he said

Partly because of how prediction markets advertise themselves, some observers now ascribe them a predictive power that’s similar to polling, or to hybrid forecasts such as Decision Desk HQ, which gathers data from a variety of sources
Sophisticated polls are a snapshot of a moment in time—a representative sampling of people indicating how they plan to vote
Prediction markets, meanwhile, derive their probabilities from the trading data of users across the world
The kinds of people who typically use these platforms are mostly young and mostly male
Kalshi and Polymarket are banned in Brazil
Is it possible that traders without much knowledge of Brazilian politics, or who had their own political biases, skewed the results? In this case, it’s hard to know
Recent academic research suggests that prediction markets are still pretty good at producing reliable forecasts even when the demographics are slanted
That’s because, in theory, the incentives of the most active traders are financial rather than political
The idea is that they bet big when they’re sure of an outcome and bet small when they don’t really know what they’re talking about, regardless of what they’d personally rather happen

For example, one Polymarket user who put $55 on Bolsonaro commented, “I LOST MONEY BUT IM SO HAPPY I DID LETS GO LULAAAA.” Still, the reliability of these markets can depend on the amount of money sloshing around
Mansour denied that Kalshi’s Brazilian-market volatility problem had to do with a lack of trading volume, but volume really only picked up at the very end; as it did, the odds started to change
Something similar played out on Polymarket
As one Bloomberg columnist pointed out , when prediction markets beat the pollsters during the 2024 U.S. presidential election, trading volume on Polymarket was in the billions
This time, the platform saw about $250 million in all
Forecasting swings like those in Brazil and Wisconsin will almost certainly keep happening
The coming U.S. midterms will be a moment of increased visibility for an already visible industry—these probabilities are now baked into some live election coverage
And once exit polls are in, real-time markets might end up filling the information gap as everyone awaits the final tally
It may not really matter whether people understand the methodological differences between prediction markets and other forecasts, or whether people understand probabilities at all
Most Americans already oppose betting on elections

If Republicans somehow stage a comeback next week despite prediction markets’ forecasts of a blue wave—if these platforms seem to miss at all—these firms may end up losing the little credibility they’ve managed to build thus far

title: How Elon Musk Turned on Ukraine
excerpt: O n October 11 , a confidential memo went out to military officers across Ukraine, urging them to brace for a catastrophe
body: O n October 11 , a confidential memo went out to military officers across Ukraine, urging them to brace for a catastrophe
Donald Trump had decided earlier that week to ease U.S. sanctions on Russia and to begin buying its diesel fuel
Based on that shift in White House policy, the memo foresaw another act of American betrayal: the loss of access to the Starlink satellite network, which Ukraine uses to operate its drone fleet

The document warned that Elon Musk, the creator of Starlink, might soon restrict service in Ukraine, and it urged users of the technology to “keep all communication alternatives to Starlink on standby—ready for immediate use—and develop contingency plans.” Two days later, the warnings began to come true
Starlink faltered across the war zone, grounding drones and halting military operations
In one case, it led to the loss of Ukrainian naval drones in the Black Sea, according to two people familiar with that mission
It came from a nongovernmental organization called Narodnyi Starlink, or “People’s Starlink,” which helps the armed forces of Ukraine acquire and operate this technology
In the memo, the group’s founder, Volodymyr Stepanets, envisioned several ways Musk could restrict service
The worst-case scenario—a total shutoff—would result in a cascade of disasters, potentially leading to Russia’s victory in the war
One senior U.S. military officer told us that “without Starlink, the war would grind to a halt.” Musk himself has suggested that might be his goal

In a series of posts on X over the weekend, he admitted to causing last week’s outages, and he lashed out at those who call for greater military aid to Ukraine. “I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict,” Musk wrote. “May you burn in hell.” Since the disruption, Ukraine and its allies have scrambled to find a replacement for Starlink, which relies on the world’s largest constellation of satellites to deliver high-speed-internet access anywhere in the world
The most promising effort in Ukraine to build such a system faced a major setback this summer, when its architect, Dmytro Stetsenko, died of apparent heart failure at the age of 46
European attempts to replicate Starlink are years away from matching its scale, and most of these efforts depend on Musk’s aerospace company, SpaceX, to launch their satellites into orbit
Russia, by contrast, has its own fleet of space rockets, and it is racing to field a network of satellites that can rival Starlink

The system, known as Rassvet, or “Sunrise,” would give Russia an “asymmetric advantage” in the war, says Andrey Liscovich, a co-founder of the Ukraine Defense Fund, which has helped secure thousands of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian military. “They will be precise enough to fly these low-cost, jet-powered drones through a window anywhere in Ukraine,” Liscovich told us
Without Starlink, Ukraine would not be able to respond
Vladimir Putin said today that Russia has stayed in touch with Musk about Starlink. “Elon Musk is a genius, really a genius,” the Russian leader said at a televised summit in Moscow

He praised SpaceX for taking the lead in the race to develop this technology. “We are only taking the first steps,” Putin said of Russia’s answer to Starlink. “We are in close touch with our American colleagues, including Mr

Musk, because in orbit it is very important not to get in each other’s way.” This account of Musk’s turn against Ukraine is based on interviews with more than a dozen U.S. and Ukrainian officials, military officers, drone manufacturers, and experts on Starlink
Most of them spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive military operations and private negotiations
Several of them have dealt with Musk and his company directly since the start of the war, in 2022, and they have seen his views on Ukraine shift from generous support to outright hostility
If anything can yet restrain Musk from abandoning Ukraine, it may be his own financial interests
His company has earned hundreds of millions of dollars from the Starlink terminals operating in the war zone
Liscovich estimates there are well over 250,000 of them
In the past, SpaceX, which runs Starlink, has reportedly charged the Ukrainian government $2,500 per terminal each month, and it has cut off service when bills go unpaid

Earlier this month, when U.S. military officials asked SpaceX about the outages in Ukraine, the company advised switching to an upgraded contract to restore Ukraine’s access, U.S. officials told us. (Musk and SpaceX did not respond to questions for this article.) In June, SpaceX held the biggest initial public offering in history, earning a valuation of roughly $1.8 trillion
Revenue from Starlink keeps SpaceX investors happy and bankrolls Musk’s other projects, including his obsession with colonizing Mars
If he pulls the plug on Starlink in Ukraine, other countries could deem the service unreliable and accelerate the race to build an alternative
But those projects will not be ready until next year at the earliest

Until then, the world’s richest man will be largely free to decide Ukraine’s fate. [ From the November 2026 issue: Choose your overlord ] W hen the war began , Musk seemed eager to help Ukraine defend itself
Russia used missile strikes and cyber weapons to take down Ukraine’s digital infrastructure in the opening days of the invasion
To keep the country online, Musk donated thousands of Starlink antennas to its hospitals, power plants, government ministries, and various humanitarian causes
Soon, the Ukrainian military began using the service to pilot its drones and stay connected in the war zone

The service provided a critical advantage: The Russians had no access to Starlink and no way to jam its signal, which allowed Ukraine’s drones to crisscross the battlefield, dropping bombs on Russian troops

Images of these attacks spread online in 2022, and they caused alarm at SpaceX headquarters in Texas. “More and more people became uncomfortable,” a former SpaceX engineer who worked on the system’s development told us
Some of his colleagues left the company in protest
Their team had designed Starlink to give people internet access in places where broadband cannot reach, like hiking trails and ships at sea, not to wage a war
In September 2022, Ukrainian officials asked him to switch on Starlink in the Black Sea
They wanted to use it in a sneak attack against Russian warships near the occupied region of Crimea

Musk refused. “Starlink was not meant to be involved in wars,” he said around that time to his biographer, Walter Isaacson. “It was so people can watch Netflix and chill and get online for school and do good peaceful things, not drone strikes.” At the end of 2022, Musk announced the launch of a service called Starshield

title: Corruption Catches Up to MAGA
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
One fundamental truth of politics is that ultimately all voter decisions come down to money

That’s why Dwight Eisenhower blew out Adlai Stevenson in 1956; it’s what James Carville meant when he declared, “It’s the economy, stupid,” in 1992; and it’s the reason that Joe Biden tried in vain to convince Americans that they were doing better than they believed during his presidency
This was also why some Democratic politicians and strategists counseled candidates not to place Donald Trump and his scandals at the center of their campaign
Better to focus on “kitchen table” issues, such as inflation and housing costs, they argued
To a great extent, this seems to have worked
Economic worries have been a consistent theme throughout the midterms, and Democrats appear poised to fare well
They’ve been helped by Trump, who has not only dismissed worries about affordability as a “hoax,” but has also gone out of his way to worsen inflation by launching a war in Iran
I wrote just last week that the economy explained GOP struggles
Yet an interesting thing has popped up in opinion surveys over the past couple weeks
A Fox News poll finds that corruption is the top issue for voters, edging inflation, gas prices, and health care

CNBC gets the same result : “Voters are now more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices, according to the final CNBC All-America Economic Survey.” The Financial Times has similar findings: “About 69 per cent of registered voters, and almost 50 per cent of those who voted for the president in 2024, said they were ‘very’ or ‘somewhat’ concerned about ‘corruption, self-dealing or conflicts of interest’ in the Trump administration.” The idea that the economy alone explained Trump’s unpopularity was never entirely convincing
He has almost always had poor approval ratings, even when presiding over a strong economy
He didn’t win the popular vote in 2016; House Republicans were shellacked in 2018, when he made the election about him; he lost in 2020; and the GOP underperformed in 2022, under his influence
He was able to win only in 2024, when the elections centered on voters’ views of the Biden presidency

One big reason for these repeated voter rejections is the miasma of scandal that follows Trump wherever he goes. “When elections are clearly about Trump and MAGA, MAGA will lose,” Michael Podhorzer, a progressive strategist, told me in 2022
Still, this finding is reassuring about voters’ discernment
My colleague Anne Applebaum has been foremost among many observers who have deemed this the most corrupt presidency in U.S. history
Even as the president and his family have made billions from his office, no single story seems to have broken through: no Teapot Dome, no Watergate, not even a Whitewater

The new polls on corruption, combined with Trump’s steadily declining favorability , suggest that rather than any single news story producing an inflection point—like the swift turn on Joe Biden after the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan—voters have just been steadily souring on the president, with corruption as one main reason. (It’s worth noting that, although the FT poll specified that Trump voters are concerned about corruption within the administration, corruption also tops lists because it means different things to different voters

Trump supporters who say they are concerned about “corruption” could be referring, for example, to “deep state” conspiracy theories.) The polling around corruption is also an indication of the success (believe it or not) of much-maligned Democratic messaging

In February, Senator Jon Ossoff began speaking about “the Epstein class,” referring to the then-recent release of materials related to the late sex offender, which sketched a clique of wealthy, powerful people emailing and socializing around the globe. “They are the elites they pretend to hate,” Ossoff said . “Trump was supposed to fight for the working class; instead, he’s literally closing rural clinics and hospitals to cut taxes for George Soros and Elon Musk.” Democrats have been using similar lines ever since
In making “corruption” a rallying cry, Democrats have found a way to yoke together a range of different stories, effectively sidestepping any division between economic issues and Trump scandals

It’s a big enough trend to fit any number of developments: Trump’s promotion of AI and data centers, despite wide public skepticism ; his focus on projects such as the White House ballroom, which is funded by donors, many of whose identities the administration hasn’t disclosed, and an arch in Washington, D.C.; his work to undermine elections
His policy toward Ukraine appears influenced by possible business ventures in Russia
His Iran war was encouraged in part by Middle Eastern allies with whom Trump family members have business relationships
Trump seems determined to help the Democrats out by boasting about oil-company profits at a time when Americans are upset about the cost of filling up their vehicles
Republicans have also bolstered the case with nominees such as Ken Paxton, a one-man alleged-graft spree
If an anti-corruption message does carry Democrats to victory in the House, and perhaps in the Senate, it will also point to how they might use Congress over the next two years
Even if they win both chambers, they will have little ability to enact policy—including actions that might help bring prices down
But a House majority alone would have investigatory power, and could use its reach to delve into Trump-administration actions that threaten both rule of law and voters’ pocketbooks

title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
excerpt: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assis
body: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools
Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond
But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business
Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments

The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all
Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%)

Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes. “There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here
It’s just not really useful in most companies today.” The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business
A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms)

It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says

It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much
But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data
He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs
Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents
But the sales raise legal and ethical questions

Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups . —Matthew King Are we there yet? Interspecies communication  Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us.  Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world
A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex

Find out how close we are to interspecies communication . —Cassandra Willyard This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter
We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue

MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century
But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp
A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating
But the chief obstacle may be one of political will
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts

( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Chinese scientists have developed a catalyst to make Mars rocket fuel It converts Martian atmospheric carbon dioxide into liquid methanol. ( SCMP ) 6 Tech billionaires have teamed up against California’s wealth tax Sergey Brin, Eric Schmidt, and others have funded a major campaign. ( Guardian ) 10 Trump now wants to ban the term “artificial intelligence” He’s demanding we all start using “Super Intelligence.” ( Gizmodo ) Quote of the day “For the next two years, we’re going to be living in a state where, on average, every week there is a critical, internet-wide vulnerability.” —Matthew Prince, Cloudflare’s chief executive, tells the New York Times that AI is currently finding software vulnerabilities quicker than they can be patched

title: 3 major issues that Republican Byron Donalds or Democrat David Jolly will need to address as Florida’s next governor

<title>3 major issues that Republican Byron Donalds or Democrat David Jolly will need to address as Florida’s next governor</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768577/original/file-20261027-63-goh1xf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=175%2C0%2C1677%2C1118&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Florida&#39;s new governor will have a lot to tackle on Jan. 1, 2027, whether that&#39;s David Jolly, left, or Byron Donalds.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">David Jolly: AP Photo/Marta Lavandier, Byron Donalds: AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein, illustration by The Conversation</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>After nearly three decades of Republican control of Florida, the executive office of the governor has become more powerful than ever before. </p>

<p>So when Florida voters choose between Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly for governor on Nov. 3, the winner will be poised to shape the state’s direction for years to come.</p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=zTrHGLoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">political scientist</a> who has lived in Florida for almost two decades and seen the powers of the governor’s office grow. I’ve been watching how the two candidates say they will use their authority to shape policy around healthcare, education and home rule – and what help they might need from the Legislature.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768258/original/file-20261026-52-tni3va.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C313%2C6000%2C3375&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="child's arm receiving an injection" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768258/original/file-20261026-52-tni3va.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C313%2C6000%2C3375&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768258/original/file-20261026-52-tni3va.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768258/original/file-20261026-52-tni3va.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768258/original/file-20261026-52-tni3va.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768258/original/file-20261026-52-tni3va.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768258/original/file-20261026-52-tni3va.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768258/original/file-20261026-52-tni3va.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Florida’s next governor will appoint the state’s next surgeon general, who will determine childhood vaccine requirements for Florida schools.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/child-receives-a-standard-immunization-at-doctor-gary-m-news-photo/2235638592?phrase=florida%20childhood%20vaccines&amp;adppopup=true">Joe Raedle/Getty Images News</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Florida health policy on vaccine mandates</h2>

<p>One of the first choices awaiting the new governor will be whom to appoint as Florida surgeon general, a position <a href="https://www.floridahealth.gov/about-us/">created in 2007</a>. The surgeon general <a href="https://www.thenationshealth.org/content/49/3/1.1">oversees</a> the <a href="https://www.leg.state.fl.us/Statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&amp;URL=0000-0099/0020/Sections/0020.43.html">Florida Department of Health</a> and <a href="https://www.wusf.org/health-news-florida/2022-02-17/has-floridas-surgeon-general-role-become-too-politicized-for-the-jobs-original-mission">county health departments</a> across the state.</p>

<p>The position comes with the power to <a href="https://floridapolitics.com/archives/473446-lawmakers-ok-bills-to-limit-surgeon-general-emergency-powers/">declare public health emergencies</a>, forcibly quarantine people and <a href="https://floridatrident.org/repeal-of-vaccine-mandates-faces-legal-challenges/">set vaccine mandates for illnesses such as chickenpox</a> that fall outside the state Legislature’s framework of <a href="https://floridatrident.org/repeal-of-vaccine-mandates-faces-legal-challenges/">seven childhood vaccine mandates</a>.</p>

<p>As part of his <a href="https://theconversation.com/ron-desantis-2-terms-in-office-fundamentally-altered-floridas-political-landscape-cementing-conservative-policies-through-strategic-control-of-state-institutions-289946">conservative remake of Florida policies</a>, Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed the current surgeon general, <a href="https://www.floridahealth.gov/about-us/leadership/state-surgeon-general/">Dr. Joseph Ladapo</a>, to the position in 2021. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ladapo emerged as a leading <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/consumer-health/health-freedom-movement/">medical freedom</a> advocate and vaccine skeptic.</p>

<p>Ladapo <a href="https://abcnews.com/Health/florida-surgeon-general-state-moving-end-vaccine-mandates/story?id=125224527">opposes all vaccine mandates</a>. At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, he <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/florida-to-recommend-against-covid-vaccines-for-healthy-kids">recommended against COVID-19 vaccinations</a> for healthy children and <a href="https://www.local10.com/news/local/2021/09/22/new-fla-surgeon-general-parents-must-decide-whether-asymptomatic-kids-exposed-to-covid-should-quarantine/">ended quarantine mandates</a> for Florida public schoolchildren exposed to COVID-19. He also said that he <a href="https://www.wusf.org/health-news-florida/2025-09-16/ladapo-tells-podcast-goal-with-the-mrna-is-for-that-not-to-be-available-to-anyone">wanted mRNA vaccines “not to be available to anyone”</a> in the state.</p>

<p>Ladapo also proposed new Florida health rules in October 2026 to <a href="https://floridaphoenix.com/2026/10/08/ladapo-eliminating-vaccine-mandates-isnt-about-science-its-about-parents-rights/">drop mandates for four vaccines</a> required for school attendance, including chickenpox and hepatitis B. Currently, the state allows <a href="https://www.floridahealth.gov/individual-family-health/immunization/parents-children-and-adolescents/exemption-from-required-immunizations/">exemptions</a> only for approved religious or medical reasons.</p>

<p>The Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics <a href="https://www.fcaap.org/posts/news/florida-pediatricians-testify-against-proposed-rule-weakening-school-immunization-requirements/">opposes the rule change</a> on public health grounds.</p>

<p>Donalds has long <a href="https://donalds.house.gov/news/email/show.aspx?ID=B5G6AKCJWTTEQ">opposed vaccine mandates</a> and says that he <a href="https://edition.cnn.com/videos/politics/2021/07/27/byron-donalds-florida-coronavirus-vaccine-cuomo-intv-vpx.cnn">did not personally receive a COVID-19 vaccine</a>. He <a href="https://www.wusf.org/politics-issues/2026-09-23/donalds-might-retain-joseph-ladapo-as-surgeon-general-jolly-says-hed-fire-him">supports Ladapo’s proposed rule change</a> to reduce school vaccination mandates and says he is <a href="https://www.wusf.org/politics-issues/2026-09-23/donalds-might-retain-joseph-ladapo-as-surgeon-general-jolly-says-hed-fire-him">open to reappointing Ladapo</a> as surgeon general.</p>

<p>Jolly, on the other hand, supports Florida’s <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/fact-check-where-candidates-byron-140433340.html">current school vaccine mandates and exemptions</a>. He says he would <a href="https://www.wusf.org/politics-issues/2026-09-23/donalds-might-retain-joseph-ladapo-as-surgeon-general-jolly-says-hed-fire-him">fire Ladapo on Day 1</a> in favor of someone who “<a href="https://floridaphoenix.com/2026/08/24/did-school-vaccines-just-become-a-campaign-issue/">embraces science and evidence-based public health</a>.”</p>

<p>No matter which candidate is elected governor, the Florida Legislature has tied his hands on how far he can push vaccine policy. The <a href="https://mynews13.com/fl/orlando/news/2026/08/14/new-federal-vaccine-guidance-raises-questions-for-florida-families-but-school-requirements-remain-unchanged">Legislature has mandated</a> measles and polio vaccines for all K-12 public school students, so getting rid of that requirement would require a change in the law. It also stripped the surgeon general of the <a href="https://news.wfsu.org/state-news/2021-11-19/desantis-repeals-the-state-surgeon-generals-power-to-mandate-vaccines">power to enforce vaccine mandates during public health emergencies</a> in November 2021, during the pandemic.</p>

<h2>Universal school vouchers</h2>

<p>One of the biggest developments in Florida K-12 education in recent years has been the creation of a system of <a href="https://theconversation.com/floridas-school-choice-program-offers-universal-vouchers-but-cannot-show-systemwide-academic-improvement-283040">universal vouchers</a> by DeSantis and the Legislature in 2023. This program allows <a href="https://www.stepupforstudents.org/scholarships/">parents of any income level</a> to use <a href="https://go.stepupforstudents.org/hubfs/Scholarship%20Info/FTC-FES-EO-PEP-Award-Amounts.pdf">US$8,000 in state money on average, based on county of residence</a>, for their children’s private or homeschooling education.</p>

<p>The universal voucher program has created intense pressure on the state budget. It cost an <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/education/2026/05/27/vouchers-grow-floridas-budget-will-there-be-added-accountability/">estimated $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2026</a>. State auditors have identified <a href="https://mynews13.com/fl/orlando/news/2025/12/04/audit-finds-fl-vouchers-program-has-trouble-tracking-millions">accountability problems</a> in tracking funds through the system. Public schools have faced <a href="https://hechingerreport.org/universal-vouchers-have-public-schools-worried-about-something-new-market-share/">declining enrollment</a>, with fewer resources to serve the neediest students they cannot turn away.</p>

<p>Donalds strongly supports the universal voucher program, recounting how his family <a href="https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2024/07/15/rnc-live-updates-coverage/donalds-talks-schools-00168551">saved money for him to attend a private high school</a>. Donalds has touted universal vouchers <a href="https://floridatrib.org/2026/07/30/what-byron-and-erika-donalds-gospel-of-school-choice-could-mean-for-florida/">in Christian nationalist circles</a> and expressed an interest in making Florida “<a href="https://floridatrib.org/2026/07/30/what-byron-and-erika-donalds-gospel-of-school-choice-could-mean-for-florida/">the model state for school choice</a>” by <a href="https://www.miaminewtimes.com/news/the-billionaire-trying-to-reinvent-florida-schools-has-a-7-5-million-bet-on-byron-donalds-40565603/">allowing parents to choose among private educational providers competing in the marketplace</a>.</p>

<p>His wife, Erika Donalds, is a former Collier County school board member who operates a <a href="https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/election/article317723535.html">network of for-profit charter schools</a> and <a href="https://floridatrib.org/2026/07/30/what-byron-and-erika-donalds-gospel-of-school-choice-could-mean-for-florida/">advocates nationally for school choice</a>. </p>

<p>The only change Donalds has proposed is a <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/teacher-pay-vouchers-candidates-florida-195700038.html">universal scorecard</a> for the voucher program so that parents can compare educational data on student performance across different types of schools. Currently, only public schools must provide this data.</p>

<p>Jolly also supports the universal voucher program but wants significant changes. Jolly personally sends his own two children to private, faith-based schools <a href="https://floridaphoenix.com/2025/09/18/democratic-gubernatorial-hopeful-david-jolly-defends-school-choice/">with the support of vouchers</a>. He says private schools that accept vouchers should <a href="https://floridaphoenix.com/2025/09/18/democratic-gubernatorial-hopeful-david-jolly-defends-school-choice/">meet the same standards and requirements as public schools</a>, including the mandate to serve students with disabilities. He also wants to <a href="https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/article317297608.html">limit private school tuition to the value of the voucher</a> and <a href="https://wusf.org/text/politics-issues/2025-12-19/democratic-gubernatorial-hopeful-david-jolly-spotlights-education-sarasota">reinstate benefit eligibility based on financial need</a>. </p>

<p>Campaign promises aside, neither candidate can do much to affect the universal voucher program, because it was created by the Legislature.</p>

<p>Democrat Jolly knows he would need the Legislature’s cooperation to advance reforms and claims that he has <a href="https://floridaphoenix.com/2025/09/18/democratic-gubernatorial-hopeful-david-jolly-defends-school-choice/">identified Republican allies</a> to do so. Donalds would likely face a friendly Republican majority for his more modest proposed reforms.</p>

<p>The next Florida governor will also be able to influence state education policy by <a href="https://www.fldoe.org/policy/state-board-of-edu/">appointing the seven members of the Board of Education</a> and then recommending a candidate for <a href="https://www.fldoe.org/about-us/commissioner/">commissioner of education</a> for that board to elect. The commissioner and state board oversee the <a href="https://www.fldoe.org/">Florida Department of Education</a> and programs from kindergarten through postsecondary education.</p>

<p>The position of commissioner used to be elected, but in 2002 voters <a href="https://floridamemory.com/learn/research-tools/guides/governors/commissioner-of-education.php">approved a constitutional amendment</a> creating the current system, which gives more power to the governor.</p>

<p>The next governor’s appointees to the Board of Education could try to shape the effects of universal vouchers more indirectly. The board <a href="https://feaweb.org/issues/education-policy/the-state-board-of-education-and-you/">could approve an annual legislative budget request</a> with new recommended funding levels for public education to make up for shortfalls due to revenue loss from vouchers.</p>

<p>They could also implement new eligibility rules for private school vouchers, <a href="https://www.flgov.com/eog/news/press/2023/florida-takes-action-against-four-florida-schools-ties-chinese-communist-party">as the DeSantis administration</a> <a href="https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/state/2026/10/15/florida-school-vouchers-could-be-banned-for-some-islamic-schools/91705943007/">has done</a>.</p>

<p>In general, Jolly says he intends to <a href="https://floridapolitics.com/archives/824559-david-jolly-famu-dei/">use executive authority as vigorously as possible</a> in education, as DeSantis did, particularly to promote diversity programs.</p>

<h2>Home rule and executive authority</h2>

<p>A third hot-button topic facing the next governor is <a href="https://scholarship.stu.edu/faculty_articles/69/">home rule</a>, or the principle that local governments, such as cities and counties, should be able to set policy on local issues.</p>

<p>The DeSantis administration severely eroded home rule. The governor signed legislation <a href="https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/state/2026/04/14/planning-law-limiting-local-governments-in-florida/89553404007/">limiting local controls over land development</a>. This bill restricted the ability of Manatee County, for example, to <a href="https://www.wusf.org/politics-issues/2025-09-08/manatee-county-joins-legal-battle-developer-friendly-law">protect wetlands</a> under the guise of emergency management legislation. </p>

<p>He also required counties to <a href="https://www.governing.com/policy/how-florida-is-pushing-for-increased-local-cooperation-with-ice">cooperate with federal immigration authorities</a> and put counties under <a href="https://www.flgov.com/eog/news/press/2025/governor-ron-desantis-and-cfo-blaise-ingoglia-highlight-excessive-local-government">DOGE-style audits</a>. He even <a href="https://floridaphoenix.com/2023/08/09/desantis-ousts-another-democratic-prosecutor-monique-worrell-of-orange-county/">removed local elected officials from office</a>. For example, he <a href="https://www.democracydocket.com/opinion/elected-by-the-people-removed-by-desantis/">ousted a pair of popular Democratic state attorneys</a>, Hillsborough County State Attorney Andrew Warren and State Attorney Monique Worrell of Orange and Osceola counties, alleging neglect of duty in both cases. By August 2023, DeSantis had removed 23 elected officials, a number <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/2023/08/09/state-attorney-is-latest-example-desantis-use-power-suspend-elected-officials/">much larger than his predecessors</a>. </p>

<p>Donalds has affirmed that he <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/09/29/david-jolly-byron-donalds-florida-data-centers-governor/">supports the steps DeSantis has taken</a> and plans to <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/09/29/david-jolly-byron-donalds-florida-data-centers-governor/">take executive authority further</a>, scheduling more DOGE audits of local government and removing more elected officials as needed.</p>

<p>In contrast, Jolly says he <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/09/29/david-jolly-byron-donalds-florida-data-centers-governor/">would counter DeSantis</a> on home rule. He <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/09/29/david-jolly-byron-donalds-florida-data-centers-governor/">wants local authorities to decide</a> budgets and policy on their own. He sees removing elected officials as an <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/09/29/david-jolly-byron-donalds-florida-data-centers-governor/">affront to the democratic process</a>.</p>

<p>What to do about large-scale data centers, however, scrambles home rule for the candidates. Donalds wants <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/09/29/david-jolly-byron-donalds-florida-data-centers-governor/">local communities to be able to decide</a> whether to build data centers. But Jolly, citing concerns about the health and environmental effects of data centers, wants a <a href="https://www.fox13news.com/news/ai-data-centers-erupt-major-battleground-florida-governors-race">statewide moratorium</a> on new data center construction for one year and is open to a <a href="https://www.fox13news.com/news/ai-data-centers-erupt-major-battleground-florida-governors-race">permanent ban</a>.</p>

<p>Voters will have an important say of their own on home rule when they vote on <a href="https://theconversation.com/floridas-proposed-property-tax-amendment-will-require-trade-offs-and-some-residents-could-end-up-with-higher-costs-287149">Amendment 3</a>, which would substantially lower homestead property taxes. Critics warn that if it passes, local governments will likely <a href="https://floridapolitics.com/archives/813837-jeff-brandes-where-amendment-3-gets-weird/">have to turn to Tallahassee</a> to make up for lost funds, and strings will be attached. </p>

<p>Donalds <a href="https://www.wuft.org/politics/2026-10-01/byron-donalds-visits-uf-discusses-dei-and-amendment-3">supports</a> Amendment 3, while Jolly <a href="https://www.nbcmiami.com/news/local/florida-amendment-3-what-a-yes-or-no-vote-would-mean/3873576/">opposes</a> it.</p>

<title>1 in 4 Pennsylvanians say they paid out of pocket for their annual checkup. Why isn’t insurance covering these preventive visits?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768303/original/file-20261026-52-6acz3u.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5200%2C3466&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Patients who think they&#39;re getting an annual checkup often end up with an unexpected bill.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/female-healthcare-provider-examining-throat-of-royalty-free-image/2224254920">The Good Brigade/DigitalVision Collection via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>I was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-17m-americans-enrolled-in-medicaid-and-aca-plans-could-lose-their-health-insurance-by-2034-260664">Affordable Care Act</a>, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing.</p>

<p>The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care. </p>

<p>Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too.</p>

<p>The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the <a href="https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation-topics">U.S. Preventive Services Task Force</a> and generally covered under the ACA.</p>

<p>When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://harrisburg.psu.edu/faculty-and-staff/park-sujeong">an assistant professor of health policy</a> <a href="https://csua.ssri.psu.edu/people/smp7048">and addiction studies</a> at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time?</p>

<p>Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers <a href="https://schaeffer.usc.edu/people/erin-duffy-ph-d/">Erin Duffy</a> and <a href="https://prevention.psu.edu/person/max-crowley/">Max Crowley</a> to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup.</p>

<h2>Why a preventive visit may come with a bill</h2>

<p>Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to <a href="https://theconversation.com/health-insurance-jargon-can-be-frustrating-and-confusing-heres-how-to-navigate-it-277355">copayments or deductibles</a>. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying.</p>

<p>The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain <a href="https://www.healthcare.gov/coverage/preventive-care-benefits/">recommended preventive services</a>, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients.</p>

<p>Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free.</p>

<p>If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible.</p>

<p>Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred.</p>

<h2>What our survey found</h2>

<p>Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1016/j.ypmed.2021.106690">face out-of-pocket costs</a> during <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1016/j.amepre.2024.09.011">preventive visits</a>. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-026-01973-5">Our study</a>, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 <a href="https://csr.hbg.psu.edu/what-we-do/lion-poll">Penn State Lion Poll</a>, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year.</p>

<p>Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50. </p>

<p>After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100. </p>

<p>Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable.</p>

<p>Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate.</p>

              <span class="caption">How doctor visits are billed doesn’t always match what service patients think they are receiving.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/nurse-checking-in-a-senior-male-patient-at-the-royalty-free-image/2252234136">adamkaz/E+ Collection via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Why these bills matter</h2>

<p>I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa070929">can discourage people from getting recommended screenings</a>. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective.</p>

<p>Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care.</p>

<h2>What patients can do</h2>

<p>Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge.</p>

<p>If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision.</p>

<p>A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed.</p>

<p>Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs.</p>

body: Patients who think they're getting an annual checkup often end up with an unexpected bill
The Good Brigade/DigitalVision Collection via Getty Images I was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand
We were discussing the Affordable Care Act , or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients
I explained that preventive care could cost nothing
Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup
He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup
I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care
Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too
The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear
I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S
Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA
When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear
I then called my primary care provider’s office
The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it
As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill
Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes
Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time? Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups
I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question
In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup
Why a preventive visit may come with a bill Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles
A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying

The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services , including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking
Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network
But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free
If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge
A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider
Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible
The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred
What our survey found Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits
But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving
We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket
Our study , published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll , an online survey of Pennsylvania adults
We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years
Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup
Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50

After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections
That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100
Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable
Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate
The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate
