<title>Some states are stepping up after federal childcare cuts – and now offer lessons for the future</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768265/original/file-20261026-52-5vsxbd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4571%2C3047&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Paying for childcare remains one of the biggest costs for households, often costing as much as housing.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/US--Rural-Child%20Care%20Deserts/81e3eb12e90640a2a762acecfc0fe417/photo">AP Photo/Craig Mitchelldyer</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>While affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-perfect-storm-of-factors-is-driving-up-us-produce-prices-but-shoppers-can-still-save-286608">from groceries</a> to <a href="https://theconversation.com/its-not-just-high-gas-prices-inflation-is-now-spreading-through-the-us-economy-283564">gas prices</a> to <a href="https://theconversation.com/us-consumers-and-businesses-are-now-facing-a-future-of-more-expensive-borrowing-291848">housing costs</a>, one important expense <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/09/universal-child-care-democrats/688794/">often gets less attention</a> – childcare.</p>

<p>After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2023/09/05/child-care-cliff-day-care/">dried up</a> at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “<a href="https://tcf.org/content/report/child-care-cliff/">childcare cliff</a>,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket. </p>

<p>The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the <a href="https://www.briefingbook.info/p/over-the-child-care-cliff">sharp cuts</a> in part by redirecting other funds to childcare. </p>

<p>But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/nyregion/mamdani-to-expand-2-k-program-on-staten-island-and-in-the-bronx.html">is expanding free toddler slots</a> for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/10/mamdani-and-hochul-bring-2-k-to-all-of-the-bronx-and-staten-isla">universal early childcare system</a>.</p>

<p>Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-caregiving-crisis-and-the-2026-vote/">signal a new willingness</a> to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families. </p>

<p>As researchers <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=KHvfS_sAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">of sociology</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=rtgPXMwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">childcare policy</a> with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from <a href="https://caitlyncollins.com/childcare-project/">our own data gathered over 75 interviews</a> with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work. </p>

<p>Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2024/2024112.pdf">more than doubled</a> since 2019. In 2024, the <a href="https://www.childcareaware.org/price-landscape24/#:%7E:text=CCAoA%20found%20that%20the%20national,which%20we%20had%20price%20data.">national average price</a> of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets.</p>

<h2>States go their own way</h2>

<p>The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/11/08/why-havent-us-mothers-returned-work-child-care-infrastructure-they-need-is-still-missing/">laid bare</a> the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape. </p>

<p>Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 <a href="https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/child-care-arp/">directed nearly $40 billion</a> to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, <a href="https://cscce.berkeley.edu/workforce-index-2024/state-policies-to-improve-early-childhood-educator-jobs/state-policies-overview/pandemic-relief-funding/">supported childcare staff</a> with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care. </p>

<p>The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to <a href="https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/occ/State_and_Territory_ARP_Child_Care_Stabilization_Fact_Sheet.pdf">220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children</a>. Many <a href="https://www.naeyc.org/sites/default/files/wysiwyg/user-73607/infant_toddler_brief_naeyc.pdf">states also provided grants</a> to create new slots and improve how providers got paid.</p>

<p>As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country.</p>

<p>One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to <a href="https://legislature.vermont.gov/bill/status/2024/H.217">pass a law</a> establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a <a href="https://www.newamerica.org/insights/vermont-needed-child-care/">decade of advocacy</a> and <a href="https://letsgrowkids.org/newsroom/vermont-public-vermont-child-care-funding-boost-payroll-tax-become-law-as-legislature-overrides-governors-veto">bipartisan support</a>, the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees.</p>

<p>Through an <a href="https://www.childtrends.org/publications/vermonts-child-care-subsidy-program-expands-access-reduces-cost">expansion of subsidies along income tiers</a>, the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while <a href="https://dcf.vermont.gov/cdd-blog/apply-now-vt-act-76-readiness-payment-program">flexible grants</a> increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About <a href="https://legislature.vermont.gov/assets/Legislative-Reports/Report-on-Act-76-Monitoring-January-2026-Building-Bright-Futures.pdf">12,000 children are now covered</a> under this program.</p>

<p>New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer <a href="https://www.governor.state.nm.us/2025/09/08/new-mexico-is-first-state-in-nation-to-offer-universal-child-care/">universal childcare</a>. Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the <a href="https://www.wsj.com/us-news/in-a-u-s-first-new-mexico-opens-doors-to-free-child-care-for-all-2dfdea96">initiative expanded support</a> to all working parents regardless of income. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Three girls draw at a table at the Children's Promise Center in Albuquerque, New Mexico." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768391/original/file-20261026-62-m15810.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768391/original/file-20261026-62-m15810.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768391/original/file-20261026-62-m15810.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768391/original/file-20261026-62-m15810.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768391/original/file-20261026-62-m15810.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768391/original/file-20261026-62-m15810.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768391/original/file-20261026-62-m15810.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Children draw at a daycare center in Albuquerque, N.M., which has gone further than any other state in expanding subsidies for working parents.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Universal%20Child%20Care%20New%20Mexico/87477f74f16e4e969ebe893e54c4cceb/photo">AP Photo/Susan Montoya Bryan</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, <a href="https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/this-state-is-the-first-to-offer-universal-child-care-heres-how-it-works/2025/09?utm_source=goog&amp;utm_medium=cpc&amp;utm_campaign=ew+performance+max-subs&amp;ccag=ew+performance+max-subs&amp;cckw=&amp;cccv=ew+performance+max-subs&amp;gad_source=1&amp;gad_campaignid=23338998931&amp;gbraid=0AAAAADfp2x3HDXKFv4pCrojxKQhrqCN7e&amp;gclid=CjwKCAjw9PvWBhAxEiwAddzYySGDM4vwEdPlyFDU6FxHXmSNFU23qpsuhN-AEx3_Wqe2t0fbyZQDFxoCkUwQAvD_BwE">the state estimates</a> that the program will save families $12,000 a year. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed <a href="https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/26rs/hb6.html">a measure with strong bipartisan support</a> to make <a href="https://www.the74million.org/zero2eight/how-kentucky-achieved-bipartisan-childcare-reform/">major investments</a> in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children. </p>

<p>The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary <a href="https://www.kentucky.gov/Pages/Activity-stream.aspx?n=GovernorBeshear&amp;prId=2751">Pre-K for All pilot program</a> in several counties.</p>

<p>Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/10/mamdani-and-hochul-bring-2-k-to-all-of-the-bronx-and-staten-isla">an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old</a> in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/nyregion/mamdani-to-expand-2-k-program-on-staten-island-and-in-the-bronx.html">has increased some slots</a>, although the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/27/nyregion/nyc-2k-child-care-programs-funding-mamdani.html">rollout in September hit bumps</a>. </p>

<h2>The childcare crunch by the numbers</h2>

<p>Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2024/2024112.pdf#page=28">a 2023 government survey</a>. That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier. </p>

<p><iframe id="0UAyC" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/0UAyC/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Bar chart showing that most families have trouble finding childcare for their kids under 5."></iframe></p>

<p>On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to <a href="https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/ERP-2023.pdf#page=130">turn many families away</a> or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant <a href="https://www.dol.gov/agencies/wb/topics/featured-childcare">costs more than in-state college tuition</a> at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the <a href="https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/childcare-workers.htm">lowest-paid workers</a> in the entire economy. </p>

<p>Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called <a href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/americas-child-care-deserts-2018/">childcare deserts</a> – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working. </p>

<p>The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the <a href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cdev.12551">learning opportunities</a> linked to children’s <a href="https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/705718">long-term development and social mobility</a>. And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent.  </p>

<p>Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays.</p>

<p>These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as <a href="https://www.bcg.com/publications/2022/solving-the-care-crisis">$290 billion per year</a> by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG.</p>

<h2>A path forward</h2>

<p>The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/05/us/politics/stay-at-home-parents-subsidies.html">preliminary proposal</a> to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, <a href="https://www.stlpr.org/show/st-louis-on-the-air/2026-09-23/trump-proposal-subsidies-at-home-working-parents-st-louis-washu">this approach fails</a> to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only <a href="https://aspe.hhs.gov/reports/ccdf-eligibility-factsheet-fy22">16% of eligible children</a> are reached today anyway. </p>

<p>We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components.</p>

<p>First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167629617305799">families make the best care decisions</a> for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also <a href="https://pn3policy.org/paid-family-leave-and-affordable-child-care-are-integral-to-a-strong-prenatal-to-3-system-of-care/">ease demand for scarce infant care</a> in the market.</p>

<p>Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help <a href="https://livehandbook.org/early-education/landscape/ece-access-and-affordability/">close the affordability gap</a> for high-quality care. </p>

<p>Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. <a href="https://vecf.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/6de6fd54-e921-4c88-a452-ad7cabccc362.pdf">Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone</a> of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs. </p>

<p>Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293665/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets
States go their own way The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families
But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape
Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare
This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care
The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children
Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid
As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own
In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents
We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country
One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement

Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support , the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees

Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers , the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care
About 12,000 children are now covered under this program
In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare
Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income
Children draw at a daycare center in Albuquerque, N.M., which has gone further than any other state in expanding subsidies for working parents
AP Photo/Susan Montoya Bryan Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028
On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year
Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure

Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children

The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options
Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties

Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K
To date, this effort has increased some slots , although the rollout in September hit bumps

The childcare crunch by the numbers Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey
That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier
On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists

<title>Falcon 9 ushered in the modern space economy – retiring it could leave the industry vulnerable</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765971/original/file-20261013-50-mrunp3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4962%2C3308&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches on April 19, 2023.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=falcon%209&amp;mediaType=photo&amp;vs=true">AP Photo/John Raoux</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://starburst.aero/news/global-orbital-launches-hit-record-high-in-2025/">More than 50% of the nearly 330 spaceflights</a> to low Earth orbit in 2025 were done on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Falcon 9 is much smaller than SpaceX’s flashy Starship rocket, but for the past 16 years it has been a reliable choice for launching satellites to orbit.  </p>

<p>It has carried payloads ranging from Earth-imaging sensors feeding smartphone map apps to environmental monitoring satellites that track wildfires. It has also launched the crew capsule that ferries astronauts to the International Space Station.</p>

<p>In late 2026, reports came out <a href="https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/09/boeing-incredibly-excited-to-serve-as-nations-only-astronaut-transportation/">that SpaceX is shuffling its staff</a> in an attempt to focus its resources on developing and commercializing Starship, while phasing out the Falcon 9. </p>

<p>At face value, this sounds like routine news; after all, companies shuffle resources all the time. But <a href="https://theconversation.com/spacecraft-equipped-with-a-solar-sail-could-deliver-earlier-warnings-of-space-weather-threats-to-earths-technologies-259877">as a space scientist</a>, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oeyIipsAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">I believe</a> that retiring this rocket threatens to suffocate the commercial space industry that it helped bring to life – unless the public and private sectors step up their efforts to fill the gap Falcon 9’s retirement has created.</p>

<h2>How did we get here?</h2>

<p>Since its inception in 2002, SpaceX has broadened access to space. In 2006, while facing the <a href="https://www.astronomy.com/space-exploration/why-did-nasa-retire-the-space-shuttle/">looming retirement of the space shuttle</a>, NASA searched for a private alternative to resupply the International Space Station. The agency <a href="https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/commercial-space/commercial-crew-program/commercial-crew-program-overview/">awarded companies</a> contracts, and SpaceX’s award helped kick-start the development of Falcon 9.</p>

<p>Despite <a href="https://www.basenor.com/blogs/news/spacex-nearly-went-bankrupt-twice-musk-reveals-the-full-story">multiple near-bankruptcy</a> setbacks, Falcon 9 made its inaugural test flight in 2010, followed by sending the SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule to its first docking at the International Space Station in 2012.</p>

<p>The real turning point came in 2015 with the <a href="https://www.space.com/31420-spacex-rocket-landing-success.html">first successful landing of a Falcon 9 booster</a>. The booster is the rocket’s main first stage. It houses fuel tanks and nine main engines. It provides the primary thrust off the launchpad but detaches from the rest of the rocket shortly after. Landing the booster meant SpaceX could recover and refly this component and <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-spacex-lowered-costs-and-reduced-barriers-to-space-112586">dramatically slash launch costs</a>. </p>

<p>In the meantime, Boeing, the other NASA contract <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-boeing-starliner-has-returned-to-earth-without-its-crew-a-former-astronaut-details-what-that-means-for-nasa-boeing-and-the-astronauts-still-up-in-space-238507">awardee, struggled</a> with <a href="https://futurism.com/space/nasa-screwed-boeing-starliner-access-space">budget overruns and operational delays</a>. Some of SpaceX’s other competitors, such as Blue Origin, pivoted toward <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvg8e5gq8ljo">suborbital space tourism</a>. As a result, Falcon 9 did more than just capture the market. It effectively became the market.</p>

<h2>A booming industry teetering on the edge</h2>

<p>SpaceX’s affordable and frequent access to space helped to breathe life into a booming space economy. It allowed startups with creative new business models to send their satellites to orbit, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/indias-takeme2space-launch-orbital-computing-satellite-spacex-rocket-2026-09-28/">such as TakeMe2Space</a>, an Indian startup exploring hosting data centers in orbit. It empowered governments around the world to dramatically expand their operations in space, including governments relying on <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/15/starshield-starlink-ukraine-restriction-explained">SpaceX’s secured communication platform, named Starshield</a>.</p>

<p>Then came the operational shift. In July 2026, <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-23/spacex-is-turning-away-falcon-customers-in-major-bet-on-starship">accounts from prospective commercial customers</a> and satellite operators revealed that SpaceX had begun turning away Falcon 9 customers to focus its resources on the more capable Starship rocket. </p>

<p>Almost overnight, the <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/30/science/starship-spacex-falcon-9-dragon">announcement threatened</a> to freeze the pipeline of launches the market relied on. Those who can afford it are paying extra to secure the few remaining slots on Falcon 9, while others are <a href="https://www.orbitalintel.org/launch/falcon-9-alternatives/">scrambling to find alternative</a> launch opportunities. While European customers are generally flocking <a href="https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/08/europe-cancels-planned-upgrades-for-ariane-6-rocket/">to the European Space Agency’s Ariane 6</a> rocket, others are booking slots on upcoming medium-lift rockets, such as <a href="https://aerospaceamerica.aiaa.org/features/rocket-labs-next-step/">Rocket Lab’s Neutron rocket</a>.</p>

<p>SpaceX is contractually obligated to continue Falcon 9 flights for NASA’s International Space Station crew rotations and other national security payloads. However, the rest of the space industry is now forced to buy into <a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/msa2lB1tGhk">SpaceX’s Starship bet</a>. There simply is <a href="https://nova.space/in-the-loop/will-super-heavy-launch-vehicles-expand-the-space-economy-or-concentrate-market-power/">no operational alternative today that can match</a> Falcon 9’s combination of high launch cadence, affordable pricing and proven flight heritage for medium-class payloads.</p>

<h2>National security vulnerability</h2>

<p>When a single company is put in charge of controlling the gate to space, its internal corporate decisions can make or break an industry. That also makes the company <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-plan-b-for-space-on-the-risks-of-concentrating-national-space-power-in-private-hands-275618">a potential single point of failure</a>, where a setback by a single vendor would paralyze the entire space economy.</p>

<p>The U.S. has dealt with this type of national security dilemma before. In the 1900s, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/money/Standard-Oil">Standard Oil owned critical oil production infrastructure</a>, pipelines and railroads. Controlling critical pipeline networks gave the company unprecedented power to set transport terms, prioritize its own shipments and restrict pipeline access for independent oil producers. This structure meant competitors had no viable alternative transport routes. Ultimately, <a href="https://energyhistory.yale.edu/political-cartoons-and-standard-oil-gallery/">this forced the U.S. government to intervene</a> because internal Standard Oil corporate decisions dictated market dynamics.</p>

<p>Standard Oil had become the gatekeeper to the free flow of oil. By addressing that potential single point of failure, the U.S. government nudged an industry to redefine itself, which led to its accelerated growth.</p>

<h2>Customers forced to pay up</h2>

<p>SpaceX took huge technical and financial bets on the success of Falcon 9. They paid off and <a href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/elon-musks-spacex-now-has-a-de-facto-monopoly-on-rocket-launches-3c34f02e">led to SpaceX’s market dominance</a>.</p>

<p>But now SpaceX wants to do it again, with the promise that Starship would help further reduce the cost of getting to space. Their vision is grand, but what happens if Starship <a href="https://www.space.com/every-spacex-starship-explosion-lessons-learned">experiences delays</a>? What happens to companies who <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/spacexs-satellite-ambitions-squeeze-out-rivals-reliant-its-rockets-2026-08-04/">relied on</a> Falcon 9?</p>

<p>As SpaceX shifts focus, competing launch providers will likely rush to take advantage of <a href="https://www.economist.com/business/2026/10/01/a-rocket-shortage-gives-spacexs-competitors-an-opportunity">this market opportunity</a> and offer rides to customers being turned away by SpaceX, but at a steep premium. The customers also face the burden of reconfiguring their satellites to fit on another rocket.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Where to go from here</h2>

<p>This sudden market shift has been a <a href="https://spacenews.com/the-rideshare-era-is-ending-small-satellites-need-anchor-customers-for-small-launch-now/">wake-up call</a>, one that I believe will cost the industry and add significant uncertainty to market dynamics in a few years. But it also offers the market an <a href="https://www.thespacereview.com/article/5319/1">opportunity to correct course by filling the gap</a> that Falcon 9’s retirement has created.</p>

<p>Over the past two decades, NASA has successfully delivered on its mandate to create a rocket-launch marketplace. To achieve this, NASA fundamentally shifted from operating government-owned hardware to buying fixed-price services. This meant that NASA became a reliable anchor customer whose contracts spurred competition among commercial providers.</p>

<p>While this model proved that routine, low-cost space access was achievable, <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/blue-origin-new-glenn-rocket-explodes-launchpad-florida/">various technical and business challenges</a> allowed the marketplace to become dominated by a single vendor. </p>

<p>Moving forward, NASA and other public agencies can work together to strategically distribute the payloads they need to launch across commercial rockets built by other companies. These government contracts can help these companies improve and <a href="https://www.fairobserver.com/world-news/fo-exclusive-a-space-revolution-is-imminent-are-we-ready/">validate their emerging rocket programs</a>. Satellite customers can design standardized payloads that work across multiple types of rockets, so they don’t rely on one launch provider. </p>

<p>NASA can also <a href="https://spacenews.com/new-nasa-office-to-consolidate-launch-procurements/">maintain its dedicated launch assistance programs</a>. Subsidizing these slots would allow smaller institutions, such as academia and nonprofit organizations, to avoid competing on the open market against large companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin that launch satellites regularly. These programs help smaller institutions that may not have the funds to directly buy their own spot on a rocket get their payload to space. These payloads are often used to give students experience and help train the next generation of space workers exploring the cosmos.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294225/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Years after she passed away, I was trying to learn more about her life before the war – something I knew very little about. When I found a book called “Sefer Kostopol” – Hebrew for “Book of Kostopol” – I hoped to find her among its pages.</p>

<p>It was a memorial book for her hometown, but beyond that, I wasn’t sure what to make of it. I’m <a href="https://www.rowan.edu/ric-edelman-college/departments/sociology-anthropology/faculty-staff/bios/rich_jennifer.html">a scholar of Holocaust memory</a>, but I had never come across anything quite like it. It was a bit like a scrapbook, with varied types of images, essays written by different residents and lists of survivors – where I found my grandmother’s name – and of their murdered families, including her mother and sister.</p>

<p>My questions led me to investigate exactly what “Sefer Kostopol” was – and to learn that communities of survivors created over 1,000 such memorial books, <a href="https://nyupress.org/9781479841271/paper-tombs/">called “yizker bikher” in Yiddish</a>.</p>

<h2>Everyday life</h2>

<p>After the Holocaust, Eastern European survivors and Jews who had left before the war created these memorial books to honor their destroyed towns and murdered loved ones. Devoted to their neighbors, these collaboratively written volumes were one way for survivors to reclaim their lives and memories.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767069/original/file-20261019-50-g1rzn3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three black and white photos arranged on a page. Each one shows a portrait of several rows of schoolchildren." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767069/original/file-20261019-50-g1rzn3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767069/original/file-20261019-50-g1rzn3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=785&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767069/original/file-20261019-50-g1rzn3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=785&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767069/original/file-20261019-50-g1rzn3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=785&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767069/original/file-20261019-50-g1rzn3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=987&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767069/original/file-20261019-50-g1rzn3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=987&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767069/original/file-20261019-50-g1rzn3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=987&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Yizker bikher were created not only to document the destruction of the Nazi genocide, but also to preserve the everyday lives that came before it. The volumes insist that Jewish communities be remembered not solely as sites of death but as places where people lived, argued, worked and celebrated. In general, around two-thirds of a given volume is devoted to describing prewar life; the remaining third includes first-person accounts of the Nazi occupation of the town and a long list of the dead. </p>

<p>Each book had anywhere from 20 to 50, even 75, contributors, who wrote in a warm, colloquial style. The visuals, too, feel personal. Photos portray the particulars of prewar life, with images of sports teams, school groups, bustling market squares and busy, modern streets.</p>

<p>Another common feature are maps, almost always drawn and labeled from memory by a survivor: the details of the forests and the rivers, the nicknames that locals used for the streets and stories of the homes and shops.</p>

<p>Beyond the photographs and maps, most volumes contain sketches by amateur artists to convey information about life under Nazi occupation. Some include art by well-known artists at the time, <a href="https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-art-and-politics-of-arthur-szyk">like Arthur Szyk</a>, a Polish-Jewish illustrator and political cartoonist. There are also ephemera like posters, budgets, song lyrics, book covers, event flyers and elementary school report cards. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767097/original/file-20261019-60-gjt8f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A tidy hand-drawn map of a small town, with labels written in Hebrew letters." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767097/original/file-20261019-60-gjt8f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767097/original/file-20261019-60-gjt8f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767097/original/file-20261019-60-gjt8f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767097/original/file-20261019-60-gjt8f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767097/original/file-20261019-60-gjt8f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767097/original/file-20261019-60-gjt8f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767097/original/file-20261019-60-gjt8f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A map of Voyslavits, Poland, in ‘Sefer zikaron Voyslavits,’ published by the Former Residents of Voyslavits committee in 1970.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Jennifer Rich</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Link in a chain</h2>

<p>The earliest volume that I studied came from Volkovisk, Belarus, and was published in 1946, just a year after <a href="https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/liberation-of-nazi-camps">the liberation of Auschwitz</a>. It’s hard to imagine survivors finding one another and putting books together so soon after the war. </p>

<p>The editors, publication committees and contributors, though, reached for a familiar model: <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/105/article/695121/pdf">the “pinkes,” the community register</a> found in every Eastern European Jewish town. These books contained everything from meeting minutes to school budgets and lists of political candidates.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767104/original/file-20261019-50-ee4mtv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="The yellowed title page of a manuscript, with writing in Hebrew." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767104/original/file-20261019-50-ee4mtv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767104/original/file-20261019-50-ee4mtv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767104/original/file-20261019-50-ee4mtv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767104/original/file-20261019-50-ee4mtv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767104/original/file-20261019-50-ee4mtv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767104/original/file-20261019-50-ee4mtv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767104/original/file-20261019-50-ee4mtv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Cover of ‘Khurbn Volkovisk,’ published by the Committee of Former Residents of Volkovisk in Eretz-Israel in 1946.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Jennifer Rich</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Like the community registers, yizker bikher have a somewhat chaotic, idiosyncratic organization to them. Both were written by many hands, and they became treasured objects.</p>

<p>The relationship was so strong that many yizker bikher include the word “pinkes” in their title. In the introductions, some editors made explicit connections between the prewar pinkes and those created in the wake of the Holocaust. One of them was Eliezer Yerushalmi, who compiled <a href="https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/novogrudok/novogrudok.html">the memorial book from Navaredok, Belarus</a>.</p>

<p>Each pinkes is a link in a timeless chain recording the history of Jewish communities, he wrote: “The present pinkes, the Navaredok pinkes, is here to tell the orphaned generation and the generations to come all that the community experienced from its very beginning hundreds of years ago to its terrible destruction.”</p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768357/original/file-20261026-52-yrq7c6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A piece of paper with writing in Hebrew and a black and white photo of a synagogue." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768357/original/file-20261026-52-yrq7c6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768357/original/file-20261026-52-yrq7c6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=752&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768357/original/file-20261026-52-yrq7c6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=752&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768357/original/file-20261026-52-yrq7c6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=752&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768357/original/file-20261026-52-yrq7c6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=946&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768357/original/file-20261026-52-yrq7c6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=946&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768357/original/file-20261026-52-yrq7c6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=946&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The prospectus for ‘Sefer zikaron le-kehilat Wielun,’ a memorial book that was ultimately published in 1974.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Jennifer Rich</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Just like Jewish communities in Eastern Europe were interconnected, so too were survivor communities in places like the United States, Canada, Israel and Argentina. Some yizker bikher committees relied on the same editors <a href="https://nyupress.org/9781479841271/paper-tombs/">and adopted features of other memorial books</a>, making the process easier.</p>

<p>The first step was for members of the book committee to circulate a prospectus to their fellow survivors to explain the memorial project. A prospectus for the “Wielun Memorial Book,” commemorating a community in Poland, was circulated in 1961, 10 years before the volume was published. The editor wrote that, </p>

<blockquote>The Wielun memorial book must be a reflection of a former home, which was so brutally destroyed and erased. In the book of remembrance, all moments, events, adventures, and experiences need to be expressed. Different facts, good deeds, memories, figures, and types. Let nothing be forgotten: days of sadness, days of joy, and hope for a better tomorrow.</blockquote>

<p>That goal – “let nothing be forgotten” – sits at the very heart of each memorial book.</p>

<h2>How they lived</h2>

<p>Despite this, yizker bikher were mostly overlooked by scholars for many years. Perhaps this was because they defy easy categories: They are too nostalgic to be histories and too historical to be literature. They are too secular to be religious and too religious to be secular. And the range of visual material complicates things even further – for example, they aren’t photo albums per se, but they certainly include hundreds of photographs.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767044/original/file-20261019-50-93rft5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C213%2C5156%2C2900&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A stack of five books with white and blue covers and Hebrew words on the spines." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767044/original/file-20261019-50-93rft5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C213%2C5156%2C2900&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767044/original/file-20261019-50-93rft5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=388&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767044/original/file-20261019-50-93rft5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=388&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767044/original/file-20261019-50-93rft5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=388&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767044/original/file-20261019-50-93rft5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=487&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767044/original/file-20261019-50-93rft5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=487&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767044/original/file-20261019-50-93rft5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=487&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Survivor communities have published more than 1,000 yizker bikher.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Tim Hawk, Rowan University</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the past few years, however, there has been <a href="https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250284334/oncetherewasatown/">a surge of academic and popular interest</a>. Scholars are <a href="https://utppublishing.com/toc/diaspora/23/2">exploring the books and the archives that created them</a> to learn more about all aspects of prewar Jewish life. They have also used yizker bikher to understand the intimate nature of the violence wrought by the Nazis and their local collaborators, and the beautiful, profound ways survivors found to honor their loved ones.</p>

<p>When we take yizker bikher seriously, it allows us to expand our focus beyond <a href="https://www.ushmm.org/learn">how 6 million Jews were murdered</a> and highlight the way they once lived. Ultimately, these books remember individuals and communities as they wanted to be remembered.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290274/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<p><a href="https://theconversation.com/as-millions-of-americans-face-a-steep-rise-in-health-insurance-costs-lawmakers-continue-a-century-long-battle-over-who-should-pay-for-health-care-271901">Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans</a> led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With <a href="https://www.healthinsurance.org/blog/health-insurance-premium-increases-for-2027-proposed-rates-by-state-and-what-consumers-should-know/">premiums expected to rise further</a> and <a href="https://chrt.org/publication/hr1-and-michigan-medicaid-work-requirements/">Medicaid work requirements</a> set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options.</p>

<p>We are <a href="https://isr.umich.edu/about/faculty-profiles/levyhelen-g/">health</a> <a href="https://michiganross.umich.edu/faculty-research/faculty/thomas-buchmueller">economists</a> who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who <a href="https://www.kff.org/health-costs/health-policy-101-employer-sponsored-health-insurance/">receive coverage through their employers</a>. </p>

<p>But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive. </p>

<p>People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks. </p>



<h2>Navigating trade-offs</h2>

<p>Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act <a href="https://www.kff.org/affordable-care-act/health-policy-101-the-affordable-care-act/">went into effect in 2014</a>, insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether. </p>

<p>The ACA <a href="https://www.cms.gov/cciio/resources/fact-sheets-and-faqs/aca-new-patients-bill-of-rights">eliminated this kind of discrimination</a>, established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also <a href="https://taxpolicycenter.org/briefing-book/what-are-premium-tax-credits">introduced income-based subsidies</a> that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established <a href="https://www.cms.gov/marketplace/about/overview-exchanges">online marketplaces</a>. </p>

          </figure>

<p>Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape.</p>

<p>Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you <a href="https://theconversation.com/health-insurance-jargon-can-be-frustrating-and-confusing-heres-how-to-navigate-it-277355">pay in premiums</a>, the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers. </p>

<p>Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious. </p>

<h2>Less costly short-term plans</h2>

<p>As their name suggests, <a href="https://www.kff.org/affordable-care-act/understanding-short-term-limited-duration-health-insurance/">short-term, limited-duration plans</a> are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons. </p>

<p>First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they <a href="https://www.kff.org/patient-consumer-protections/examining-short-term-limited-duration-health-plans-on-the-eve-of-aca-marketplace-open-enrollment/">may not provide the full range</a> of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses.   </p>

<p>Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans. </p>

<p>Because of a concern that they <a href="https://www.commonwealthfund.org/publications/fund-reports/2018/mar/state-regulation-coverage-options-outside-affordable-care-act">destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers</a>, short-term, limited-duration plans are <a href="https://www.kff.org/patient-consumer-protections/examining-short-term-limited-duration-health-plans-on-the-eve-of-aca-marketplace-open-enrollment/">banned in five states</a>.</p>

<h2>Alternatives that look like insurance</h2>

<p>Another seemingly affordable option is <a href="https://www.commonwealthfund.org/publications/fund-reports/2018/aug/health-care-sharing-ministries">healthcare sharing ministries</a>, arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance. </p>

<p>Because they are not <a href="https://www.kff.org/patient-consumer-protections/health-policy-101-the-regulation-of-private-health-insurance/">regulated as insurance companies</a>, healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also <a href="https://kffhealthnews.org/courts/sham-sharing-ministries-test-faith-of-patients-and-insurance-regulators/">no guarantee</a> that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim. </p>

<p>Like short-term, limited-duration plans, <a href="https://chir.georgetown.edu/health-care-sharing-ministry-data-point-to-problems-for-consumers-regulators/">healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage</a> based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits. </p>

<p>Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is <a href="https://www.benefitspro.com/2025/08/22/aca-alternative-farm-bureau-health-plans-sprout-in-14-states/">health coverage offered by a farm bureau</a>. These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture. </p>

<p>These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by <a href="https://kffhealthnews.org/health-care-costs/farm-bureau-plans-less-pricey-alternative-aca-coverage-tradeoffs/">screening out high-cost consumers</a>. Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/DBTmNm8D-84?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Choosing a health insurance plan often requires fighting through a thicket of jargon.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What should you do?</h2>

<p>Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option. </p>

<p>If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for <a href="https://www.kff.org/interactive/subsidy-calculator/">a premium subsidy</a>. And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections.</p>

<p>If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself:</p>

<p>Make sure you ask for a <a href="https://www.cms.gov/cciio/resources/fact-sheets-and-faqs/indexsummarybenefitscoverage">summary of benefits and coverage</a>. This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage <a href="https://www.healthreformbeyondthebasics.org/the-summary-of-benefits-and-coverage/">are required to provide</a> this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance. </p>

<p>If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive. </p>

<p>Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/03/ftc-sends-nearly-100-million-refunds-consumers-harmed-benefytt-technologies-sham-health-plans">multiple</a> <a href="https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/ftc-simple-health-judgment-sham-insurance/707214/">cases</a> in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance.</p>

<p>Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293327/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Republicans have an Epstein problem
excerpt: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, a Democrat, speaks at a public exhibit about the Epstein files in Dallas. | Chitose Suzuki/The Dallas Morning News via Ge
body: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, a Democrat, speaks at a public exhibit about the Epstein files in Dallas. | Chitose Suzuki/The Dallas Morning News via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Eighteen years after his first conviction, and seven years after his much-debated death, the ghost of the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein is suddenly inescapable again.  He’s the subject of scores of midterm campaign ads, each more lurid than the last
A second bill mandating the release of the Epstein files is currently kicking around Congress

And on Monday, House Democrats released a new report alleging that the Justice Department helped cover up details of Epstein’s relationship with President Donald Trump, calling — very aspirationally! — for an independent criminal investigation
Of course, no one really expects Trump’s attorney general to name a special counsel to investigate the Trump administration

In a statement, one White House spokesperson panned the report as “a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans.” (The timing, just one week before the midterms, does seem pretty fortuitous.) The document, which runs to 50 pages, draws on public accounts and staff interviews with an unspecified number of survivors, including a former pageant queen who alleges that Trump raped her in 1993

The woman had previously accused Trump of groping her, which a Trump spokesperson dismissed at the time as “fake.” Go a little deeper View Link When it comes to Epstein, however, Democrats don’t need a lot of new material to damage Trump

The scandal, and his administration’s handling of it, continue to cast a long, dark shadow over Republicans.  That’s surprising to me, candidly, because the decades-old dealings of even a very despicable sex offender don’t have any bearing on Americans’ day-to-day costs or experiences

And Trump has been able to brush off a lot of other unsavory behavior and associations.  But the Epstein story has lodged in the brains of some voters who helped elect Trump — including  young voters whose growing disillusionment could make a big difference in next week’s elections

Many of these young voters “resent the fact that Trump’s basically become part of the establishment” and see the Epstein files as evidence of that, the political analyst Rachel Janfaza recently told Vox

Some  also feel burned by Trump’s campaign promise to release the government’s investigative files on Epstein…and his about-face once in office .  Democrats, sensing an opening, are hammering the issue

According to data from the tracker AdImpact cited by NBC News, there are currently more than 500 campaign ads airing across the country that include the words “pedophile” or “predator.”  Many of them reference Epstein or the so-called Epstein files, and three-quarters are backed by Democrats

One recent ad featuring an Epstein survivor, and targeted at Kansas Republican Roger Marshall, slams the incumbent senator’s September 2025 vote to block a procedural measure that would have released the Epstein files. (The Senate later moved to release the files by unanimous consent.)  Another ad, this one in Maine, claims that Epstein’s “business partner” funneled $3 million to Sen
Susan Collins’s super PAC. (Importantly, the connection between Epstein and this purported partner is so tenuous as to be nonexistent.)  These ads will fade after Tuesday, of course
But you haven’t heard the last word on this

Should Democrats win control of either chamber, they’ll gain the power to subpoena witnesses and documents for yet more Epstein investigations.  Some Democratic leaders in the House are already salivating over that prospect
One link for later ➨ Ask better questions than “what do you do?” Small talk is often dominated by idle chatter about traffic, weather, or jobs
To actually get to know your conversation partner, try leading with questions that get at their interests : what a friend’s friend is reading, for example, or what a barista’s favorite beverage is
You can even draft a little list of go-to questions in advance to deploy in conversation when you need them
Just don’t treat the exercise like a checklist

The real key to better small talk is being curious.  Before you go… Did you know… that concrete is the second-most-used material on Earth? (The first is water!) Mixing and pouring concrete is responsible for a huge share of global emissions, but there are efforts underway to make it more sustainable
Today’s trivia: An arroyo is a stream — or at least, a streambed — found in what type of environment? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the name of the lovable yellow dog in the comic strip Garfield
That would be Odie, whose look evolved over the years as illustrator Jim Davis sought to distinguish him from his iconic canine rival Snoopy.

title: The HBCU renaissance, explained
excerpt: Many historically Black colleges and universities have seen record-breaking enrollment numbers in their recent freshman classes
body: Many historically Black colleges and universities have seen record-breaking enrollment numbers in their recent freshman classes
But on the flip side of that surge, Black freshman enrollment is actually down by 27 percent among the top 50 most selective institutions in the United States
And there are some big explanations behind these shifts

As the landscape of higher education has evolved from the eras of segregation to the civil rights movement to Trump-era racial politics, Black students have had to adapt on college campuses nationwide as government mandates, school policies, and the dismantling of affirmative action have impacted their education over the years.  Hosted by Kahlil Greene , this video is part of our new series, Kahlil Explains , that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society
This first episode traces the history of HBCUs and the experience of Black college students to unpack why Black student enrollment is growing at HBCUs yet declining at other elite institutions

title: How big should Democrats go on childcare? We asked a potential 2028 contender.
