body: Andy Beshear, who is weighing a presidential run, told Vox that he believes Congress “should take action to make sure that every state provides pre-K for 4-year-olds.” | KC McGinnis/Bloomberg via Getty Images The midterms are racing to their conclusion, but the presidential contest is right around the corner
As the next primaries begin to take shape, how Democratic hopefuls intend to address childcare is already shaping up to be a major question.   Kentucky Gov
Andy Beshear, who is weighing a run for president , is one of the potential contenders with hands-on experience around this issue
Facing Republican opposition in the state legislature, he recently redirected federal funds to launch a pre-K pilot program , standing up 3,000 new seats since May
And he believes national Democrats should be making a push to expand access to preschool as well

We wanted to better understand not only how Beshear is thinking about early childhood initiatives, but also his approach to spending on new federal programs more broadly, and what he’s learned from past efforts to expand access to families that failed
On Tuesday, we spoke with Beshear remotely about his work in the state — and his message to Democrats outside of it
Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity
Since 1991, Kentucky has supported voluntary preschool, yet today still only about a quarter of 4-year-olds can attend the state-funded program
Why has it been so hard to make preschool available to every family who wants it? Well, it shouldn’t be hard
You know, pre-K is an opportunity for every child to get off to a good start
And right now in Kentucky, because of the history you just mentioned, over half of our Kentucky children show up not ready for kindergarten
So before they’ve ever walked into a public school they are already behind.  So why has it been hard to make that happen? Well, so at least in my tenure, somehow pre-K has become political
You know, 4-year-olds aren’t registered to vote
They’re not Democrats or Republicans
But I’ve pushed every year to get this in the budget
We can easily fund it given that I’ve produced a surplus every year I’ve been governor, yet our Republican leadership simply will not let it happen
So, as you mentioned, there have been attempts at expanding this before
What have you learned from those earlier attempts, and what are you doing differently now? So it’s interesting you bring that up
The same leadership that will not pass pre-K funding in our current budget cycle voted for it under the last Republican governor, but won’t vote for it under me
The last Republican governor vetoed the expansion , and they expressed their displeasure
So the only thing that’s changed here is the party of the person in charge
And what I hear is our Republican leadership saying they don’t want to give me a win, but they’re willing to hand a loss to all of these 4-year olds
But for me as governor, I don’t get to accept excuses
So what I’ve done is I’ve taken flexible workforce training funds called WIOA funds , which you can use for a lot of different things
They’re used in a number of states for pre-K
And we have launched five pilot programs in different parts of the Commonwealth that are already a stunning success.  The smallest county in Kentucky is called Robertson County and has zero childcare
You have to drive 40 minutes one way or an hour another way just for any form of child care

It’s one of the places we started this and just to see the parents and the impact that it has on them — most of those parents don’t share my political party — but this is a great opportunity for them that they’re embracing.  It sounds like it’s gotten pretty polarized in your state

When you talk with Republican lawmakers privately, what do they tell you about why they won’t support expanded preschool? Well, many rank-and-file Republicans in our state legislature want pre-K, and a number of them helped us to push for it this time
But leadership that’s been here for far too long and gotten far too partisan is simply blocking it at this point
What we need is for it to get to a vote, because this is the top polling education issue among Republicans
If we had ballot measures and we put this on there, it would pass 80-plus percent because everyone wants that opportunity for their children

My hope is now that we have started these pilot programs, including one in Franklin County, which is where the seat of government is, that they can go and see how good this program is and not allow the next set of 4-year-olds or the next set of 4-year-olds or the next set of 4-year-olds to miss out on it
But I’m gonna do everything I can with the funding that I can find to provide as much of this opportunity as possible
So there’s a lot of speculation about whether you might run for president
Without asking you to make any announcements here, I wanted to ask how you’re thinking about these issues nationally
You recently called yourself a more “practical” candidate when explaining your concerns about Medicare-for-all

When you look at something like childcare or pre-K from a federal perspective, what does being practical mean? I think it means that there is a role for the federal government, and I’m supporting a number of congressional candidates right now and talking to all of them about pre-K

When people talk about the different sides of the Democratic Party — which I think is an overblown story, but still — like when Elizabeth Warren and I get together, we try to find some different things that we both agree on that we could work together on, and pre-K is one of those areas, so is housing. “I do believe that Congress should take action to make sure that every state provides pre-K for 4-year-olds.” I do believe that Congress should take action to make sure that every state provides pre-K for 4-year-olds

title: Humans can coexist with AI. Here’s how.
excerpt: It feels like the skies above our AI-frenzied world have darkened in the past month
body: It feels like the skies above our AI-frenzied world have darkened in the past month
Employees at Anthropic and Google started quitting , citing fears that the AI was spiraling out of control

After a string of agents started hacking websites , researchers used AI to discover vulnerabilities in critical systems, leading to large swaths of the web going dark last week and giving rise to a scary term: Black October
At the same time, as it continued to ramp up AI spending, Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees — over a quarter of its workforce — and economists once again warned of a bubble
Yet, a lot has happened recently to make AI genuinely useful for more people
AI Agents are getting better and can now make restaurant reservations for you
Walmart made it possible for agents to shop on behalf of humans , a bold move since Amazon banned the practice
Apple announced an AI-ready home display that can turn on your lights

And let’s not forget that AI is also helping scientists find cures for formerly incurable diseases and mathematicians solve previously impossible problems .  It’s hard to reconcile the incongruity between the recent bad news and good news
For most of us, the state of AI is anxiety-inducing — especially when it comes to our livelihoods
According to a Pew Research Center study published in August, 71 percent of Americans think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the next two decades
That figure is up 7 points from where it was two years ago

Sure, in the best-case scenarios, AI could erase inefficiencies at work, streamline our daily lives, cure diseases, and generally improve the human condition.  But what if you are the “inefficiency” at work that gets erased? That tension is at the heart of Ethan Mollick’s latest book Co-Existence: The Next Phase of AI
If there is such a thing as an AI sage, it would be Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School and faculty director of its Generative AI Labs
To the nearly half a million subscribers to his Substack newsletter, One Useful Thing , he delivers semiweekly updates from the jagged frontier of the technology’s development
His message in any medium is resoundingly clear: You need to use AI in order to understand it

And to get the most out of using it, he argues that you have to accept that AI is not going away; it’s only going to become more important.  That ethos doesn’t make the existential threats of AI any less daunting, but that’s not the point
Unless you’re an early Anthropic employee or a United States senator, there’s probably not much you can do directly to rein in AI’s potential harms

But you can, according to Mollick’s worldview, decide how the technology could fit into your life and think about how you fit into an AI-dominated future.  I recently spoke with Mollick about his new book, what life and work might look like in the agentic AI era, and what it means to be an artisan when even knowledge is industrialized
His theories about living with AI are meant to help you navigate the future, regardless of the latest forecast. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity
We’re entering a new era for AI, and the vibes are different
AI agents are something that many of us will encounter, interact with, and maybe even embrace
I’ve always known you as someone who jumps on the cutting edge of this technology to figure out what it can do
What do you think most people don’t understand about the next generation of AI? I really think people haven’t internalized what agents do
Agents mean many things, and we can talk about personal agents, like Muse
But the fact that the problems that plagued working with AI agents before — you had to guide them each step of the way, they made mistakes, hallucinated constantly — that’s kind of gone
You can regularly get hours, days, weeks of work out of a system.  It’s not just a theoretical thing anymore
I talk to coders all the time who are a hundred times or more productive than they were before

And in other fields, we’ve kind of moved past the theoretical discussion about AI being, “This is going to be a big deal,” to, “It’s here.” From a whole kind of co-intelligence perspective, we’ve gone from, “Here’s how we use AI and work with a chatbot back and forth,” to, “These systems are now doing real work in ways that matter to real people and are reshaping real fields for better or worse.” And if you’re used to using AI a year ago, if you’re not paying for one of these systems, it’s really easy to have lost track of what’s going on

What about the practical, everyday ways that AI is disrupting our lives? And what do you think are the limits of that disruption? So outside of the job world and homework cheating, I think life has changed only a little bit for people, partially because these systems were kind of complicated to use and you had to decide what you were using them for
But I think the advent of personal agents, like Muse and Dot, are going to lead to a very rapid change in a lot of ways
Most people I know who aren’t experts who use these systems, like my parents, are using these things spontaneously
They’re finding that once you know how to prompt the AI to do something, it can do things spontaneously and come back to you because it has your email and everything else
Just as one example, I was unable to figure out how to cancel my standing $8 a month wifi subscription from my airline, and I was like, figure this out

And it went to customer service, joined chats, then I have no idea what it did, but now I don’t have a subscription to wifi anymore, thank goodness.  “I deeply worry that if I de-skill myself entirely, I won’t even know how computers work.”  So there is this sort of lowering friction piece that’s super interesting, with good and bad elements to it

The bad side of lowering friction is both that every article gets written by AI, so there’s no human thinking in it anymore, and that companies don’t want 10,000 customer service agents coming to them demanding new things
So I think we’re just on the edge of seeing the mass change in everyday life
Right now, AI is a really good second opinion on everything
As agents become more popular, they start to take action
How do you know when to let AI do the work, though? We know that offloading certain tasks to AI can make you worse at doing those kinds of tasks in the future

title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
excerpt: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence
body: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence
Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers
Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover
The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look
A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how
That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business
The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing
The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth
Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant
Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful
For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record
They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made
Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated
When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor
More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows
But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity
Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products
When intelligence participates in action Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world
By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor
Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action
Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions
Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station
Vision can help the system assess a part’s position
A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement
Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits
The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately
The same principle applies to quality operations
When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers
The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%
The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in
This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential
Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment
Simulation offers a way to examine proposed actions before applying them to equipment
Manufacturers can explore how a change might affect a process in a digital environment
That does not remove the need for physical validation, but it creates room to learn without treating the production line as the first experiment
Responsible deployment, therefore, begins with operational discipline
Leaders need to establish clear authority or what systems may change, reliable connections to equipment, defined safety boundaries, and a record of decisions and actions
People must be able to recognize uncertainty, intervene, and bring equipment to a safe state
Trust rests on those practical arrangements, not on confidence in a model alone
More capable machines, more capable people Manufacturing has long combined human ingenuity with increasingly capable tools

title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
excerpt: Solid-state transformers do more with less: By swapping bulky steel cores for advanced semiconductors, solid-state versions can be one-tenth the size of convent
body: Solid-state transformers do more with less: By swapping bulky steel cores for advanced semiconductors, solid-state versions can be one-tenth the size of conventional transformers while absorbing the jobs of multiple devices—and losing half as much energy in the process

Data centers are the proving ground: Companies like Heron Power, which raised $140 million earlier this year, are targeting data centers first, where voltage requirements are lower and the money is flowing—with a California factory set to hit full production by 2029

High-voltage transmission remains the hard part: Solid-state transformers still can't handle the hundreds of thousands of volts needed for long-distance power lines, meaning the technology's biggest test—and biggest opportunity—is still ahead. " data-chronoton-post-id="1147684" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid
The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply

And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.  As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers
New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure
Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits

Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity.  These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission
But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid
The grid’s backbone Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat
How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost
So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down.  Consider, for example, your local solar plant
For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant

Enter transformers.  In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines
Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer
Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood

If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home
Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire
The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel

Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core.  The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down
When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core
That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage
This process is called magnetic induction
Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University
In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them
That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety
The problem is that today’s transformers are big and bulky, and they’re also difficult and expensive to replace, Lukic says
A solid option Solid-state transformers essentially add so-called power electronics—semiconductors that convert and control electricity to the typical blueprint of today’s transformers
While a conventional transformer operates at the frequency of the part of the grid it’s connected to, a solid-state transformer actually controls the frequency of the current

Typically, a solid-state transformer first converts incoming AC power from the grid to DC power, and then to a higher-frequency AC power using switches made of a semiconductor like silicon carbide.  From there, a magnetic component changes the voltage

Because the advanced semiconductors allow transformers to exert so much control over the frequency and stability of the current, the magnetic core can be much smaller than in a conventional transformer
Some come in at roughly one-tenth the size but have the same capacity, Lukic says
Finally, additional power electronics convert the electricity from high-frequency AC to its required form—generally back to DC power and finally to lower-frequency AC
Today, stepping voltage up and down is many transformers’ only job
But solid-state transformers can do much more

They absorb the jobs of devices like rectifiers and inverters (which convert AC to DC power and vice versa), shrinking the total footprint of the electrical equipment and potentially cutting the amount of power lost in the system
In August, the New York Power Authority and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) tested a one-megawatt solid-state transformer under realistic utility conditions at EPRI’s test site
The device was built in Lukic’s lab, and it was the first such test for a transformer of that capacity, he says
The prototype was roughly 98% efficient—meaning it lost only 2% of the energy fed in
An equivalent conventional transformer and rectifier, by comparison, would be about 96% efficient together, Lukic says
